title: How Blood Pattern Analysis Works
summary: Valentine's Day-themed episode of Stuff You Should Know on blood pattern analysis (blood spatter analysis). The hosts open with a joke origin story of Valentine's Day cards, then discuss how analysts read blood evidence: the types of weapons, handedness, victim position, time since death, and clotting. They explain the three spatter velocity classes (low, medium, high) with their force thresholds and typical causes, including passive spatter, projected arterial blood, back and front spatter, internal muzzle staining, and voids. They cover string-based angle reconstruction, the trigonometry for calculating impact angle from drop elongation (width divided by length, then arcsine), and modern 3D software. History covers Eduard Piotrowski, Paul Kirk and the Samuel Shepard case, and Herbert MacDonald, who helped found the International Association of Bloodstain Pattern Analysts in 1983. The CSI effect is discussed. The episode closes with the Lindy Chamberlain case, where blood evidence and handling problems figured in her conviction, and a listener mail story from a medical student.

segments.title: Valentine's Day opening and blood spatter setup
segments.summary: The hosts open the Love Edition with a joke origin story of Valentine's Day cards, then tie the heart symbol to blood and introduce blood spatter analysis as a topic.

segments.title: Dexter, analysts, and what blood evidence reveals
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the TV show Dexter and whether real analysts are photographers too, and note that blood pattern analysis is as much art as science and corroborates other evidence. They list what it can reveal: weapon type, number of blows, handedness, victim position, whether death was immediate, and time since death from clotting.

segments.title: Low, medium, and high velocity spatter
segments.summary: The hosts explain the three spatter velocity classes. Low velocity is gravity-driven drips under about 5 feet per second, often from stabbings, including passive spatter. Medium velocity, from blunt force or arterial spurting, is roughly 5 to 25 feet per second. High velocity, usually gunshots, is over 100 feet per second and carries tissue and bone.

segments.title: Muzzle staining, voids, and gunshot details
segments.summary: The hosts discuss gunshot-related evidence, including internal muzzle staining and stippling from close-range shots, which can draw blood back into the gun, and voids, which are shadow shapes left where something blocked the spatter.

segments.title: Reconstructing angles with strings and trigonometry
segments.summary: The hosts describe the traditional string method, where strings run from each drop to a convergence point that approximates the victim's head position. They then explain the trigonometry of impact angle: divide a drop's width by its length and take the arcsine. They also mention modern 3D software, No More Strings, and how juries respond to animation.

segments.title: History of bloodstain analysis
segments.summary: The hosts trace the field's history: Eduard Piotrowski's early work on head-wound bloodstains, Paul Kirk's analysis in the Samuel Shepard case, and Herbert MacDonald's 1971 book and training, which led to the founding of the International Association of Bloodstain Pattern Analysts in 1983.
topics: International Association of Bloodstain Pattern Analysts

segments.title: The CSI effect
segments.summary: The hosts explain the CSI effect, in which juries expect TV-style forensic science and a prosecutor who cannot deliver it may lose the case.

segments.title: Lindy Chamberlain case and blood evidence
segments.summary: The hosts recount the 1980 disappearance of baby Azaria Chamberlain at Ayers Rock, Australia. Blood evidence on the jumper was mishandled, an expert testified about a cut throat, and Lindy Chamberlain was convicted. Years later a missing jacket was found near dingo lairs, and the Chamberlains were cleared, with legal fees costing about a third of the compensation.

segments.title: Listener mail: lingering from a medical student
segments.summary: A listener named Brooks, a fourth-year medical student, shares an ER story about a patient who stole his own blood from a lab to fake a kidney stone and convince staff he had blood in his urine.

segments.title: Sign-off and search tips
segments.summary: The hosts suggest searching How Stuff Works for blood pattern analysis, invite listener stories by email, and close with a sponsor line.
